Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a teacher, what is the harshest truth a student has ever taught you?
Answer: I was teaching a freshman Calculus course for Biology Sciences, and accidentally overheard a heated discussion between some students in between classes. One of them was a Muslim student called Anand, and he ferociously objected to the theory of evolution (which was obviously very important in the Biology curriculum). One of the professors had explained the evolution of movement in seahorses — a complex and rather mysterious research domain which utilizes theoretical mechanics and differential geometry — and as soon as the word “evolution” had been mentioned, Anand rejected every word of it. Upon being asked by another student whether those really were Anand’s honest thoughts — even though he had seen abundant proof of the contrary — Anand clearly hesitated and said: “I am simply not allowed to think otherwise.” It revealed the shocking truth that this young man was fighting against choices he did not want to make, but somehow he had started to understand that what was (really) going on in Nature, was vastly different than what had been taught to him since childhood. Still, his hesitance showed that a seed had certainly been planted in the mind of this young man. And maybe, just maybe this one would germinate. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIPHY.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: A person has told me that chemotherapy and radiotherapy are toxic and deadly, that they can give me a cure for my cancer through natural medicine. Is he right?
Answer: The herbal treatment. I know of at least two people who tried it (instead of classical cancer therapies), and they are the exact two people who vanished in the most painful way. One was a patient of my girlfriend. A young man with a peeing problem that turned out to be a prostate thing. He wanted to have many more girlfriends libido-wise, he wanted to perform, he did NOT want to wear diapers, he wanted to be erected, he wanted to be a man (in his own language). And he declined. He declined every single therapy (prostatectomy, psychiatric evaluation and help, hormone treatment) because his brother would prepare herbal emulsions and the like to cure him. And surprise, surprise — he turned into pieces under the supervision of his loving brother who did not know squat. The second subject is an actress called Sylvia Millecam.[1] A Dutch icon know for her uncanny talent to improvise, fast intuition and beauty. But Sylvia also had an uncanny obsession for (her own) beauty, and she would do anything to keep it that way. A mastectomy ? — no thanks (‘they” define me as an actress). Chemotherapy ? — how will I look afterwards ? So Sylvia, as an avid supporter of alternative medicine, chose to follow a guru who claimed to cure cancer and every single other disease known to mankind through her own radiating radiation into water (usually recorded months in advance) and through radio talk (also usually recorded months in advance), and her guru urged her to stop having classical medical treatments, and drink her radiated water, and listen to her radiated words instead. At a not-so-small cost, as you might have expected. And Sylvia died before she reached the age of 45 — the tumor had ruined her body as if a bomb had exploded.[2] She was a mere skeleton. She was a mere copy of a thought. She was someone who could have been saved, but who believed the herbal woman with that very big fee. These are some of the few people I have known who tried the natural course. And who were obliterated on the way. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: If you were a patient, what would you do if you felt your doctor was rushing you through your appointment?
Answer: Just the other day, my girlfriend told me a horrific story about a patient who was basically neglected by his former urologist. The 42-year-old patient had been diagnosed with testicle cancer and was nervously waiting for therapies to begin, but for some obscure reason his urologist did not make the time to come up with the appropriate medical answer, and brushed the patient off as soon as he frantically entered the consultation room yet again. And so the patient decided to ask for a second opinion in another hospital. When my girlfriend gave him a physical last Friday, she indeed found the tumor in his left testicle — it had considerably grown, and the testicle was bound to be removed. But after further inspection, she also felt a lump in the other testicle which had not been detected by the patient’s former urologist. And this testicle has to be removed too. Fortunately the patient already has children, but in any case some nontrivial permanent hormonal treatments are awaiting him to prevent him to become a female essentially, plus the psychological weight of a life without testicles (which might sound funny, but definitely is not). So if you really think you are being rushed through your appointments by your MD — certainly if something serious is lying beneath — you may want to ask for a second opinion. It’s your life after all. SOURCES: Anatomy of the penis (Gray’s illustration).[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what has a patient done that caused you to burst out in laughter?
Answer: The patient was wheeled into the ER with a broken hip, only 52 years old and looking even much younger. And still, something was going on. The surgeon on call told the nurses that the patient had to stay in bed until the operation, and that no matter what, this patient might prove to be a nuisance. Less than thirty minutes later, the patient asked one of the nurses what he was doing in the hospital, and demanded that he leave ASAP — “There is NOTHING wrong with me !” And so the nurse explained that he had an accident and broken his hip, and that he must stay in his bed at all costs until the operation. The patient did not understand his predicament, and became even angrier because he was obviously held here against his will, and for some reason he had forgotten what had happened earlier this week. But in any case, one thing was sure (because he was not crazy): “He had NOT broken his hip, and he was leaving the hospital ASAP !!” And then he jumped off the bed. At first, some of the MDs laughed the whole issue away when they heard about what had happened, but soon after they understood that the patient really had jumped off the bed. And they all knew what happens to a broken hip when it hits the floor again. But this particular patient suffered from young on-set dementia, and he simply forgot what he was told, and then reacted as if he never heard the question. He never had a broken hip though. (Those crazy people.) SOURCES: the medical scans were taken from The Lancet.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: People with autism who got diagnosed (really) late, what was a dead giveaway you didn’t notice was autism related until you got diagnosed?
Answer: I know I should not do this, but I am doing it anyhow. There is not a single person (with autism) who can answer this question. Which means that any single person who answers this question as an autistic person, is actually not autistic. Let’s first translate the question into a more physical-medical context: “People who got in a wheelchair really late, can you please walk to me to explain when you noticed you could not walk ?” They can’t. Because they can’t walk. They can’t take a stroll because the legs don’t work. (“There was this car accident, you know.”) And autistic patients can’t either. If they suffer from REAL autistic spectrum disorder — with REAL, I mean that as a paraplegic, you don’t have any feeling in your legs so you can’t walk around with a stick — they cannot answer this question. Because real ASD patients do not understand that they have a disorder. The saddest Quora accounts are those which say (in the heading): I am autistic, and proud of it (2,300 answers). Patients — the REAL ones — with ASD do not understand that diagnosis. Do not write answers about their disorder, because the not-understanding is a part of the diagnosis. If you understand and write about it, you don’t have it — not really. If you are able to walk in one way or the other, you are not paraplegic. So, please-please-please, so-called autistic writers on Quora: I know you need attention, and I know you need a way to be special (for some reason). But this is not the way. It’s hard enough to not feel your legs. SOURCES: drawing by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do contractions hurt during labor?
Answer: A colic occurs when there is an obstruction within a hollow internal organ, such as the intestines, gallbladder, rectum, kidneys, ureters, and uterus. To try to get rid of the obstruction, the smooth muscles inside the walls of the hollow organ contract vigorously around it, and these spasms cause pain. These smooth muscles are involuntary (we cannot control their function) and are controlled by the unconscious part of our brain function using the autonomic nervous system.[1] (In some way it’s our instinct that govern the colic.) And this is where our story gets really interesting. Most people attribute the intense pain associated to labor mainly to the stretching sensations of cervix and uterus, but that is definitely not so: sensory denervation of the uterus occurs during pregnancy and cervical sensory denervation occurs at the onset of labor, so that actually there are no such stretching sensations whatsoever during childbirth — the stretch receptors are totally gone.[2] But where does the actual labor pain come from ? Labor pain occurs due to vasoconstriction within the uterus. When the uterus contracts, there is a reduction in blood flow to the uterus causing hypoxia:[3] This decrease in blood volume causes pain because although the uterus is denervated, the surrounding blood vessels remain innervated, and the disruption of homeostasis causes an imbalance in the system, which results in sensations of pain. So the original “uterine colic” is the bad guy — he (eventually) causes the pain. On a related matter, renal colics are generically considered to be (much) more painful than “uterine colics,”[4] and to add insult to injury, the psychological strength of the pregnant patient determines a big part of the personal perception of childbirth pain. (The lower the pain threshold, the worse the perception.) That’s one reason why the breathing method really works. And although natural childbirth is usually very painful, it is not the worst pain in the world, nor the most painful medical condition in the world — of course. Otherwise, who would go for a second baby without an epidural ? SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the image: Emile Beau: Grossesse gémellaire. Ouvrage: Atlas complémentaire de tous les traités d'accouchements, Edition: Paris : Masson, 1865. Auteur: LENOIR, Adolphe, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Question: What has an actress refused and was controversial?
Answer: Jamie Lee Curtis always refused to address her medical condition — and this is perfectly okay — but she also never denied it. It was a birth defect, and so what. You see, technically she was born like a man, but medically she appears to have something called Testicular Feminization Syndrome (TFS) from birth:[1] This is precisely the effect in testicular feminization syndrome -- there are internal, undescended testes and no uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, but externally the labia, vagina, and clitoris all develop. Typically, the labia and clitoris are indistinguishable from those of a normal (46, XX) female, but the vagina is shorter than usual or sometimes absent. Breast development is that of a normal woman, and so are many other sexual characteristics of body habitus, such as pelvic shape. Armpit and pubic hair are markedly decreased or absent. And very importantly: patients with TFS cannot have children. Personally, I do not care at all what her congenital disorder is, because I think she looks absolutely terrific — especially in the 1985 movie Perfect, in which she/he really looked perfect to me. But maybe you, dear gentle man and gall, are disturbed by me mentioning her/his early predicament, while it won’t change an iota of her almost perfect characteristics (and I know many of you agree). Is an X, or an Y, really that important here ? — You tell me. SOURCES: the footnoted site. (For the photograph: Jamie Lee Curtis at the 1980 Canned festival.)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What are some sad truths about life?
Answer: Nicole is the 74-old-mother of one of my best friends, and on Saturday she had a long talk with us because she needed someone to talk to. It was at the birthday party of her grandson — who also is my godson (terrible term) — and her oldest sister was there as well. Aunt Lynn, a proud educated woman of 87 whom Nicole considers to be her mom, rather than her sister. Aunt Lynn has been a single and extremely independent woman for most of her life, and I have known her at a personal level for at least fifteen years. But something has changed. She still drives a car, but since about a year, she often gets lost when she tries to visit her little sister (only a couple of blocks down the road), and has to drive back. She always dressed meticulously in the past, following old etiquette rules, but nowadays she often walks around in her pajamas, not really realizing what she is doing. Or what day it is. She also virtually stopped bathing. My friend’s family is conservative, and the word “dementia” has never been mentioned in conversations — she “forgets a lot” and “has a hard time remembering what she was talking about” — but not the word (as if saying the word will only make matters worse). The last time I saw Aunt Lynn (before Saturday), it was unclear to me how bad her memory was affected by her condition, and also on Saturday, I thought she was doing really well for a 87-year-old. Until she ordered drinks. All of a sudden, she grabbed my friend — her nephew — by the arms, and ordered drinks for some people. And on the verge of being aggressive, she urged him to hurry up, because she was tired of waiting. We thought she was kidding at first. Only, she wasn’t. Her sister Nicole was extremely worried (because the mental deterioration of Aunt Lynn has progressed really rapidly in the past months), and she tried to convince her sister to call it a day, and head back home with her. But Aunt Lynn refused altogether, and stated “that this was HER house, and that SHE would decide what happened IN HER HOUSE.” Only it wasn’t her house at all — it was my friend’s. She never lived there (not even close). In the end, Aunt Lynn was so confused that she joined her little sister to go back home, speechless and confused, as if she was a toddler who needed a nap. And I saw the tears in Nicole’s eyes, and realized that an era was nearing its very gloomy end. And that nothing will be left of Aunt Lynn’s mind apart from scraps and pieces, wrapped up in aggressive episodes of frustration, while every next tick of the clock will obliterate her even further, and every next question will confuse her even more. And that is the saddest thing about Aunt Lynn. That if she will even take a few more steps down the ladder of oblivion, suddenly all letters and sounds will be lost, and only the bleakest emptiness will remain — And with any luck, one last smile. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov.

Question: As a doctor, have you ever accidentally and inappropriately laughed at a patient?
Answer: This happened to a patient in my girlfriend’s hospital near the end of April. The patient was only 52 years old, and suffered from a rare case of young-onset dementia. He had been wheeled into the ER with a broken hip. So the surgeon on call told the patient that he had to stay in bed until the operation (for obvious reasons), and he also warned the nurses that since the man was suffering from young-onset dementia, they might want to keep an extra eye on him. In the beginning he was still a bit drowsy, but less than thirty minutes later, the patient asked one of the nurses what he was doing in the hospital — “There is NOTHING wrong with me !” And so the nurse told him the truth: that he’d had an accident and broken his hip, and that he must stay in his bed at all costs until the operation. To which the patient screamed “that he had NOT broken his hip, and that he was leaving the hospital ASAP !!” And then he jumped off the bed. SOURCES: the medical scans were taken from The Lancet.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was your best moment as a doctor?
Answer: An 83-year-old man and his wife entered the consultation room. The woman explained that her husband often got up at night to pee — sometimes five or six times on a single night — and so she was wondering if his prostate needed a check-up. After an interview with the patient, a digital rectal check and further medical investigations (such as blood tests to determine his PSA levels), the old patient’s prostate appeared to be in an excellent state. The patient’s wife was really surprised, because he often even peed “with less-than-ten-minute intervals,” night and day. The urologist had thought about this a great deal, and so she decided to change tactics, and give it one last, but very different shot: “Mister Redding, can you tell me what day it is ?” The patient’s spouse did not understand and was utterly perplexed. Mister Redding answered: “Why, it is Monday doctor !” But actually it was Thursday. The urologist then took a piece of paper and a pencil and asked Mister Redding to draw a clock, put in all the numbers, and set the hands at ten after eleven. And he simply could not do it. The urologist’s eyes met the eyes of the patient’s wife, and read the question the old woman was trying to ask, not understanding what was happening all of a sudden. And so she answered. “Mrs. Redding, your husband does not have prostate cancer — which is good. But most probably he has been suffering from Alzheimer’s for a while.” Of course, this still had to be verified by a neurologist, but the case was almost crystal clear. And that’s why he had been peeing so chaotically — he simply constantly forgot that he had already peed. Mrs. Redding, first still perplexed, but then more relaxed, admitted that in hindsight this actually made a lot of sense, and it explained many small changes in his daily pattern which actually turned out to be symptoms now. And more than anything else, she appeared to be relieved. Because the doctor “had solved more than twenty questions at once.” (And it wasn’t cancer after all 🙂) SOURCES: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What hard truths of life does everyone need to realize?
Answer: It was an evening in November, and the crickets stopped making any noise. It wasn’t really cold, but Summer was certainly over. We decided to have a quick drink in a pub, because I had to leave for a while the next morning. In the restaurant, everything felt okay. In the car afterwards, the mood had quieted down. As if it had never been there. I remember we talked about trivialities, but only later I realized that my trivialities mattered a great deal to her — that is to say, my every wording of everyday (non-)problems hit her very hard. As if I was an enemy. And here is a simple truth: I did not notice her reaction at all. This was small talk, and I thought we were doing okay. The actual cool down would come within an hour. After we had hit the ice berg. One. Fucking. Hour. And I can say this to you: I knew we hit it, in the car, when driving back home. I realized more than everything else that we had hit something. Something invisible that took away the skin, but left everything underneath to bleed, something invisible that I could almost touch, but did not feel at the time being. We were sinking. The ice berg would surface only many months later, but I knew that suddenly there was pain while I could not see a wound — she was keeping it hidden from me. And in the months that followed — the months in which she proceeded to develop her relationship with a lover — I tried to keep the sinking pieces afloat with all my (legendary 😉) might, but the water was too cold, and while I was looking for a door to climb onto, they had already reached the shore (and forgot about me all along). So yeah, the water was cold, but it also wakes you up. And when I woke up, I knew what I had to do. And I also knew it meant I had to fight my ex-lover who had turned venomous on me. This was more than a decade ago. Hundreds of thousands of dollars in between. And a cancer that spread, and that ended her life. But not mine. SOURCES: the drawing is mine.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what's the saddest experience you've had with a patient?
Answer: The name of the disease sometimes reveals more than it is hiding, even when it’s very rare. The urologist had never seen it before in a patient — only in university text books and the like. The patient was 75 years old, and he was suffering from severe pain in the groin. His condition (increasing pain, a bad fever, and local discoloring) was deteriorating too fast. And the urologist knew immediately what it was — only one condition looked like this, and grew so quickly. FOURNIERS GANGRENE. An acute necrotic infection of the penis, scrotum or perineum (necrotizing fasciitis), which essentially is a flesh-eating disease with an extremely high mortality rate. Less than 1/50,000 males (and some females) get it, and most of them eventually die from it.[1] The man was basically rotting at an exceptionally fast rate. The urologist tried to save the old patient’s life by removing as much rotted tissue as possible from the infected area, including the man’s entire penis and scrotum, but the gangrene had already grown beyond those borders, and kept spreading at a mind-blowing speed, obliterating all tissue it passed through until soon there would be nothing left to obliterate. When the man awoke, the urologist — almost in tears — explained that he only had a couple of hours left (at best), and that he needed to say goodbye to his loved ones, now that he still could. The man gave her a faint smile, and whispered: “Thank you so much, doctor. I am completely ready to go, and I am so glad the agony will be over soon.” There was no time left to say goodbye to his loved ones though. Question: As a doctor or nurse, have you ever caught your patients doing something inappropriate?
Answer: This happened only yesterday. As a urologist, you see many unexpected patients with unexpected stories, but some are even more surprising than others. This patient was a middle-aged man with a wife and kids, and he had a problem downstairs. His testicles were swollen and slightly wounded, and so was the skin of his glans penis. My girlfriend felt that the patient was hiding something, and asked him to tell the entire story — not a selected part which blurred the bigger picture. He hesitated for a while, but then opened his backpack to take out a device, while he obviously was getting a wee bit aroused (but she tried to ignore it). A little metal birdcage with a round opening at the back — my girlfriend had no idea what it was. “It’s a chastity cage. To put my genitals in. I wear it at certain parties, and it’s the only thing I wear at those parties.” It was the kind of party his wife did not know about, and he liked to keep it that way. The cage was the obvious culprit of his genital condition, and my girlfriend did not even try to ask what the cage was for. But this was obviously one for the books. A patient with a secret life, wounded, and aroused. And caged like a bird in more than one way. Question: Has a nurse been inappropriate to you?
Answer: He told it without the least bit of shame, wrapped into medical language, and hidden under his most serious urological poker face. Not all the people sitting at the table were urologists (nor doctors, for that matter), so they trusted his professionalism. And that was actually the precise mechanism behind it — using his medical specialism to “earn” the trust of his female patients, and then proving to be the helping hand he always was and is. A good man. A digital artist. Literally, that is. Because this doctor — a man with a wife and children — blatantly stated that he always performed digital vaginal examinations on his patients, and even insisted on doing it to his teenage patients as well, “in order to know the patient’s vaginal profile a little better.” Without any medical indication whatsoever, this is a crime disguised as an examination, and he knew this all too well. The sheer number of patients that have been treated by his helping hand runs in the triple digits, and he thoroughly enjoyed digitally touching every single one them, as the little droplets of sweat on his upper lip seemed to indicate. Because this touching doctor knows how his patients think, how they put their entire body into the hands of their medical shepherd, and how, in the end, nothing can go wrong — In Doctors, we Trust. Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is a paranormal thing/creature that scares you the most?
Answer: The Wendigo. A mythological creature originating from Algonquian folklore which possesses human beings, and causes its victims to suffer from an insatiable hunger and the desire to murder humans and eat their flesh.[1] The spooky and really intriguing part of the story is that Wendigos truly exist. Wendigo psychosis is an extreme case of cabin fever in which affected people start killing other people — often their loved ones or crew members — and then eat them. One of the most famous examples is the case of Swift Runner, a Plains Cree trapper from Alberta. In the Winter of 1878, his family was starving and his eldest son died. Only twenty-five miles away from emergency food supplies (in a Hudson’s Bay Company post), he butchered his wife and five remaining children, and ate them. When he came back in Spring and walked into a nearby Catholic mission, the fact that his entire family was missing arouse enough suspicion for him to be investigate — and he confessed in the end what he had done. When he led authorities back to the crime scene, what they found was staggering:[2] There were bones everywhere, some broken in half and hollowed out. That could only mean one thing. Someone had snapped them open and sucked out the marrow. Their suspicions were confirmed when they found a pot full of human fat. He was hanged on December 20, 1879. The Wendigo was gone for now — But not for long. SOURCES: the footnoted sites. The image on the right was created by JDMS-Alistar through DeviantArt, and the image on the right was found through Google images.[3]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most terrible thing you've heard of that happened to your child?
Answer: This happened to a friend of ours (and it happened to her child). She had noticed one early morning that some hair was wrapped around one of the fingers of her baby boy. It’s called a “hair tourniquet”: human hair (or some other type of thread) tied around a finger, toe, or male genital — usually this happens to very young children during the night. And usually things turn out all right, but as the term “tourniquet” suggests, the affected digit cannot receive an adequate blood supply, nor can blood be drained through the veins. So it can go wrong — in rare cases the digit even has to be amputated. In the case of our friend’s baby, his little finger top looked so badly swollen and discolored that she immediately tried to free the finger. And she succeeded in unwrapping it, but not much later her baby started to convulse, and went into cardiac arrest. When the paramedics arrived, there was nothing they could do. By removing the hair tourniquet, most probably a blood clot from the finger top was released into his little body, and caused severe thrombosis in the end. (A fatal sepsis caused by gangrene in his finger was an alternative possibility, but less likely.) The only thing she wanted to do was helping her baby as fast as she could. And she killed him instead. SOURCES: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How did you react when you discovered that your spouse was cheating?
Answer: In the final phone conversation I had with my ex-wife before she filed for divorce — that is to say, she finally admitted on the phone that she had been cheating all along, and that she had decided she wanted a divorce — she did not mention any detail. Not who. not why, not when. “Dear Thomas. When I was contemplating our marriage, I happened to meet someone, and one thing led another, and I developed feelings of love for him. So, you know, I want a divorce.” She did not even dare to tell me in my face — she waited till I was abroad for work, and then called me up, while she was taking stuff from our house. I was shocked. And in Germany. I asked her right away with whom she had been cheating on me. She immediately answered “that in her head, she had never cheated on me since she considered our relationship to be over before she had started her new relationship.” (She only forgot to tell me.) That is how cheaters always think, by the way: they are always innocent. After I repeated my question a number of times, telling her I had every right to know after all the things she had done, she said his name. (And she knew that he was the one I had suspected all along.) And when I asked her — blatantly — when they slept together for the first time, she again turned to silent modus because every new truth made her a worse person. “On my birthday. We first met in Bluesette.” Bluesette was the pub where we had met on our very first date. It was then that I started to realize that she was ruthless, that by the very act of meeting with this man in “our place,” she was erasing me from her past. She was creating new truths, and I had to be obliterated. And that was just the start. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIFer.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Doctors and nurses, has a patient ever diagnosed you and been correct?
Answer: The patient enters the consultation room with her mom. She has genital warts and does not know how they got there. Her mom is also clueless about the cause of the itch. Lisa is 14 years old. Her mom is 30. Lisa’s boyfriend is also part of the gang, and the urologist immediately notices that he has genital warts as well. On his tongue and lips, that is. The urologist knows that this will be a long, long day. Lisa and her boyfriend have been sleeping together since Lisa was twelve years old, and without any form of protection. Her mom has no problem with this whatsoever — in fact, she humorously adds that she was only a little bit older when she had her first “real” boyfriend. (As the urologist can count, she is not really surprised.) They have no idea what STDs are, nor what protection is good for. When the urologist asks Lisa some standard questions, it turns out that Lisa does not know how babies are made (Lisa: “I know you can get pregnant if you swallow some semen, because my best friend Mary-Beth became pregnant when she did just that. And she was still a virgin.”) Then, after some specific questions, Jerry admits outright that he might have had some fun with some women of ill repute — unprotected, of course, since Jerry does not know what STDs are, and protection ruins all the fun. While he was with Lisa, by the way. And both Lisa and especially her mom do not really mind because “boys will be boys, and Jerry is a man.” The urologist suddenly blurts out that Jerry is NOT a man, that it’s totally irresponsible for kids to sleep together if they do not know how these things work, and what the consequences are, that some STDs are really dangerous, and that this kind of behavior could lead to Lisa getting pregnant while she is just a child. Lisa’s mom looks at the urologist, and says: “Well, if that is your opinion, then maybe YOU are the one with a problem, and YOU should be a better mother than me, if that’s that what you’re saying. Maybe YOU should be the one who talks to a professional because I am a bad mother, if that’s what you are saying. Maybe YOU should help Lisa, if I am so bad, if that’s what you are saying.” And for once, the patient of ill repute might be right. SOURCES: Dissection of the uterus in the latter stages of pregnancy, showing the foetus, placenta and umbilical cord. Colored line engraving by W. H. Lizars, ca. 1827. Wellcome collection.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What has been the most unusual family secret you’ve discovered after getting older?
Answer: It was well known that my paternal grandfather’s mother had worked for a while, as a maid, at the court of a famous European king. But what some family members also found out that as a single woman, she became pregnant from a man who was not in the picture. And weirdly enough, in a strongly religious Catholic society in which unmarried mothers were seen as sinners and shameful subjects who were often hidden in maternity homes or convents to save their family’s reputation, she was not fired at all. Instead, she even received extra help to make ends meet, and she was allowed to keep working in the palace after she had become a true unwed mother. So those family members (my dad’s oldest brother, his wife and their son) concluded that she had a special protected status because the king must have fathered the child who would later become my grandfather. And they keep persisting on their theory, and never fail to mention my uncle’s and cousin’s royal blood whenever they can. My side of the family rather takes this comical idea with a grain of salt, and we have never seen any resemblance between our family members — in particular my grandfather — and members of the royal family whatsoever. Except the Habsburg chin, of course. SOURCES: Google images.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Have you ever been invited to dinner at someone's house and you were not served any food?
Answer: We knew them quite well, so when they invited us we were sure the evening would be a ball. And that was an understatement in all the many meanings of the word. The starters were really very good, and after the starters they proposed we go sit in their royal jacuzzi “and have entrees and desserts in the water.” We had no idea what they meant, but when our hosts completely undressed and jumped in the water, we were kind of startled by the food they had to offer. Eventually we ended up in the jacuzzi as well (they had bathing suits), but when our hostess served us new portions of champagne while showing off her bosomy character near my face, I felt my ex-girlfriend stiffening (and not in a good way). Our hostess only smiled, and sat down nicely beside me, while her husband was fetching a new bottle of champagne. My ex-girlfriend was even more shocked when she saw him running after the bottle, and then coming back, dancing like a dervish while completely standing still. Still, I felt her hand down there in the pool, so I thought she was easing up because these people were good people really, and because besides their exhibiting, they gave us enough free space to feel comfortable. The fact that my ex-girlfriend was much more assertive than usual was also a surplus. She was not like that at all. Never was. In the end, we dressed up again after too much champagne, and went back home. The jacuzzi had been a winner, and rarely had an unplanned enterprise ended so well for me — be it under water, with not enough food but certainly enough liquid. Our hostess waved us off with a generous smile. When I enthusiastically alluded to our secret encounter in the water, my girlfriend looked at me as if I was demented, and so I dropped the subject altogether because I knew this conversation was going nowhere. And I remained silent in the car for the rest of the ride. (She was a bosomy soul indeed.) SOURCES: Shunga Ukiyo-e woodblock print by Keisai Eisen (1790-1848), c. 1825.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do some people dislike you for literally no reason at all if you have been kind and decent and engaging?
Answer: One month ago, my daughter received a message from Esther, a girl in her 6th grade class. It said that “she was de-friending every single person of the class, because they had hurt her soul so many times, and she simply did not need them anymore.” (They are all going to middle school now, and most of them to different schools. Esther has made a decision at the very divide of their young lives.) It sounds like a sad dramatic story in the make — Esther, whose soul was tortured by the other kids. But we also know Esther’s mom (who is the spitting image of her daughter). And Esther’s mom is toxic. And she poisons her daughter. Esther’s mom has no friends, and she is convinced that the world is against her. That she is a victim. But Esther’s mom is hiding something — especially for her daughter. And the thing she is hiding is the fact that she wants to be a victim, that she wants to complain about the fact that ishe s all alone in the world — she is the martyr in her own carefully devised life story. And that Esther has to be a victim too. My daughter once was invited to Esther’s house and play with her in the afternoon, and we gladly accepted the kind invitation, because making new friends — Esther was new in school — is fantastic. When we came back to get our daughter, Esther’s mom said: “We will probably not see you again, I guess, because that’s how it always goes. I guess Esther won’t be invited by you to come and play with your daughter, but that’s the way it is.” She really believed she was a victim, but she victimized herself. And her daughter. And seeing how she is molding her own daughter into martyrdom, I think it’s fair to say she is bordering Munchausen-by-proxy — she psychologically tortures her daughter in order to get the attention, and especially the pity she so deserves. We did not know what to say (because people like that never hear what you are saying), and while we were waiting for our daughter, Esther’s mom mentioned the fact that her son — Esther’s little brother who had gladly played along — had COVID. “But I thought I better not mention it, because otherwise you would not like us.” (Sigh.) Esther is twelve years old today, and she is de-friending everyone else in 6th grade. Because she is convinced that nobody likes her, that everybody hates her for some invisible reason. (Later, we found out that Esther had to change schools because “nobody liked her.” Double sigh.) But Esther has become the mirror image of her mom — she refuses to join in games “because nobody wants her to join anyways,” she refused to go to birthday parties “because nobody wants her at the party anyways.” Esther is a Munchausen-by-proxy victim, already completed distorted by her mom. And things will only get worse. SOURCES: the art is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Do nurses wear diapers?
Answer: The answer is NO (I take it that you mean during long surgeries), and I am highly surprised and somewhat taken aback that someone answered positively on this question, claiming he/she wears them systematically during operations which take 10 hours and more. Defecation and all. (My guess is that this person is a pervert.) In any case, of all the OR nurses and doctors we know, none of them ever wears a diaper — not even when they are still coping with the aftermath of a bad stomach flu and the like. All these people are highly trained professionals, and all these people know exactly when they can leave the table, and when they cannot. And just to be very clear: in situations which involve high stress (and great responsibility), your bowel movements and bladder summersaults are controlled by a first-things-first mechanism which simply is stronger than your basic instincts. In such cases, your mind does not leave any elbow room for No. 1 and No. 2 — The life of the patient comes first. SOURCES: Whoisjohngalt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I have a hard lump deep in my inner thigh that I just discovered, and when I push on it, it hurts. What could this be and how worried should I be? Is it a tumor?
Answer: At first it was a lump — not in her inner thigh but under an armpit. It did not worry her at all, but just to be sure she called her GP and made an appointment. The GP gave her a physical, and just to be sure, he scheduled some medical imaging and blood tests. (For him, the fact that the patient’s aunt had died young from breast cancer was kind of a red flag. Keep that in mind.) This is what a good GP should do — assess all possibilities. The results weren’t any good. Breast cancer, stage unknown. The lump was not a tumor, by the way, but a swollen lymph node. Because that’s where the cancer had traveled to, and that was not a good sign. Lymph nodes are hubs through which cancer can spread to other, more distant parts in the body. So further tests were needed to determine the stage, just to be sure. Those results weren’t any good either (and that is an understatement). The many black dots on the images were tumors, scattered across her spine, and the stage was known now. (This was a patient whom I used to know intimately, but I only heard about the details in an even later stage.) Less than 4 years later, she would succumb to her condition. The cancer had spread to the liver as well, and had obliterated her body and mind until nothing was left except for the final, empty gaze. That is not necessarily what will happen to you, of course. A lump usually is innocent, but as you understand now, it could also announce a far darker story. So you should go to your GP and have your case examined as soon as you can — Just to be sure. SOURCES: painting by Adida, through DeviantArt.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Is there someone who got real life superpowers after an accident?
Answer: Most people think that he was born this way, but that is not the case. His world-famous characteristically ambiguous eyes were actually the result of a fistfight in the Spring of 1962 with a good pal (called George Underwood), causing so called Anisocoria — a condition in which a person has different-sized pupils:[1] “Underwood’s fingernail had scratched the surface of Bowie’s eyeball, paralyzing the muscles that contract the iris.” The iris of David Bowie’s left eye was permanently expanded, giving him the famous blue and green/black eyes look — and so actually his eyes really had the same color, although they looked so very different. And I’m certainly not claiming that he would not have become the musical super hero he grew into without the Anisocoria, but his eyes were a very important defining part of his enigmatic and chameleon-like persona, and very often the devil is in the details when it comes to legends and the like. In David Bowie’s case, it all boiled down to one argument with a friend in 1962, which would alter his destiny and change his looks forever — Through a lucky punch. SOURCES: the footnoted site. Photo: CA/Redferns.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I am 45 years old. I have no children and have never been married. What is the point to being here?
Answer: My uncle was 40 when his father, whom he lived with, almost died from a bowel obstruction. Although my grandfather survived the emergency surgery and his one year stay in the hospital (a major part in intensive care), he never was the same again, and had to move to a nursing home. For my uncle, a new world opened — a world of freedom. He never married the girl he wanted to marry — she chose another man, and it broke his heart. And he never had children, but he had us — his nephews and nieces. And after his father (who was a tyrant) had moved out, he started to travel without the constant guilt that his father was all alone in the apartment. And he discovered the wonders of the world. My uncle is 75 now, and his health is giving him a rough time, but he still travels (although not that far). In the past years he met a new love in his life in the guise of orchids, every which way. And he systematically started searching rare species in the wild, photographing them in detail and musing about his discoveries in the many writings that he always e-mails us. There’s always a good reason to be here — even if you feel lonely — and lightning could strike in the most unexpected way, and even in the marvelous guise of a bowel obstruction. (Ask my uncle.) SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do doctors ignore patients when they tell them what they think might be wrong with them?
Answer: Just the other day, my girlfriend told me a horrific story about a patient who was basically neglected by his former urologist. The 42-year-old patient had been diagnosed with testicle cancer and was nervously waiting for therapies to begin, but for some obscure reason his urologist did not make the time to come up with the appropriate medical answer, and brushed the patient off as soon as he frantically entered the consultation room yet again. And so the patient decided to ask for a second opinion in another hospital. When my girlfriend gave him a physical last Friday, she indeed found the tumor in his left testicle — it had considerably grown, and the testicle was bound to be removed. But after further inspection, she also felt a lump in the other testicle which had not been detected by the patient’s former urologist. And this testicle has to be removed too. Fortunately the patient already has children, but in any case some nontrivial permanent hormonal treatments are awaiting him to prevent him to become a female essentially, plus the psychological weight of a life without testicles (which might sound funny, but definitely is not). In my personal opinion, some doctors postpone therapies or even totally ignore the patients’ obvious problems for the sake of convenience, because other patients are more lucrative or because they have no idea how to help the patient without the help of other doctors (and then the ego sets in). So if you really think you are being rushed through your appointments by your MD — certainly if something serious is lying beneath — you may want to ask for a second opinion. It’s your life after all. SOURCES: Anatomy of the penis (Gray’s illustration).[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: How long can a woman keep a fetus (dead or alive) in her body?
Answer: Not very long. Actually, it has to be removed as soon as possible, since a stillborn baby is essentially a a mass of dead flesh — and we know what dead flesh does in a moist environment of 99°F, right ? One of our friends experienced exactly that: one day, she felt that her baby girl stopped kicking, and over the weekend, the baby remained ever so silent. She knew something was wrong, and went to her OB/GYN as soon as she could. The message was harsh: her baby had died in the womb at seven months. It was her first pregnancy, and the only picture of her daughter was taken right after birth, where the baby lay lifeless and pale in her arms, as if sculptured in marble like Michelangelo’s Pietà. (I’ve seen the picture, and it was absolutely devastating.) [In the post Roe vs Wade era, some women — such as Deborah Dorbert (photo) — are forced to carry their non-viable baby to term, which is even worse. Deborah’s baby boy died in her arms immediately after birth, without kidneys.][1] In the days before labor was induced, our friend suffered from immense psychological trauma, because she did not feel inside what she was supposed to feel, and because she realized what she had become, and what she would always be, no matter how she would look at it in the future — A coffin of flesh for her own deceased daughter. SOURCES: the footnoted site. Painting by Stephen Early.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As an attorney, have you ever experienced a case that made you re-evaluate your life?
Answer: Two years ago, a befriended attorney told me during a wedding dinner that the hardest cases he dealt with were the child abusers — some of them had even killed an underaged child (after or during the abuse). He had children of his own, by the way. Another friend of ours (she was an MD, of all people) shouted: “They should KILL all of them !” My friend-attorney did not agree. He kindly told her that everyone has the right to be defended, whatever dark deed they had done. Our friend did not agree. (“They should be TORTURED as well !!”) He proceeded with explaining that almost 80% of child abusers had been abused themselves as a kid, and that although they had turned out to become assailants (and even murderers), they also had been victims, and still were. Most of them hated themselves for what they had done (knowing how traumatizing it was). The other 20% consisted of sick people — psychologically so twisted that every day was a fight against demons they did not understand (and most often they lost). Talking to his clients had totally changed his perspective on these people — people who had committed violent and depraved crimes, who had taken someone’s innocence for good, people who had even killed. But above all, even they were human beings. (“He had never met a monster, after all these years.”) Our MD friend did not even listen anymore, and shouted that every single child abuser should be castrated (she assumed they were all men, which they aren’t), and then hanged. She lived in a black-and-white world, though. He did not. SOURCES: for the image, I consulted Tales of Times Forgotten.[1]

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the saddest thing a patient has said to their doctor?
Answer: A couple of days ago, an old woman was wheeled into the ER because she was suffering from a bad urology-related infection. My girlfriend was not on call, but on Monday she acquired more details about the patient in order to decide what would happen with the patient. It turns out she is paraplegic, blind and all alone — “I have no family, no friends, and I do not feel connected to the world anymore. Would surgery really help me at this stage ?” And she is right. Another operation would further deepen her medical predicament (which is already so very bad), and would further alienate her from her surroundings if she even survived. And that wouldn’t be fair. So it wouldn’t be okay to open her up again. She has suffered enough already. SOURCES: image AI-generated by Stable Diffusion on Prompt Hunt.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is done in secret among nurses?
Answer: Doctor hunting. There is a universal phenomenon in hospitals in which some female nurses actively try to develop a relationship with one of the hospital doctors. The status of such nurses becomes higher when they are married to a doctor (in the end), and as silly as that sounds, it’s an undeniable truth. And as silly as it sounds again, doctor hunters who eventually find their prey, often (but not always) act very differently than “common” nurses — they have a powerful husband now, the husband earns a lot of money, and the latter basically lifts them into another part of society. And so they become arrogant. Some of these doctor hunters are very hard to work with — it is as if they cannot hide the fact that hubby is a medical doctor, which has to make them more important than “ordinary” nurses, right ? One of the big hospital secrets which is always hushed away on TV is that there is a well-defined hierarchy in hospitals, and in that hierarchy the doctors are the pilots and the nurses the flight attendants. Every single hospital employee knows this, by the way. On the other side of the spectrum, we have the nurse doers — doctors that actively search for (secret) relationships with nurses. Some of them utterly enjoy the experience (nurse after nurse after nurse), but never plan to end their marriage in favor of the nurse. The main entry stays at home. In my girlfriend’s hospital, a rather impressive number of (doctor hunter, nurse doer)-couples are known, and some of them are “secret” (because the doctor has a family back home), and others are not (because they got married in the end). In one instance, we witnessed to nurses — both doctor hunters — fight at a party because they found out that they both had a relationship with one and the same doctor (who had a wife and kids). They weren’t even mad at him — only mad at each other ! 🙄 It’s always interesting to see how twisted hospital shows misrepresent what really happens in a hospital, and what I find most striking is how totally different nurses are represented compared to real-life situations. In the end, the truth still is that a doctor title opens doors — And doctor hunters want the key. SOURCES: Plate 6, Surgical anatomy of the axilla. Wellcome Collection. (© Public domain)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Which celebrity (stars) had a secret that was finally revealed?
Answer: It was a birth defect, and so what. It was a bit messier when she was a child, but as she grew up, Jamie Lee Curtis turned into a marvelously looking person. Technically Jamie was born like a man, but medically she suffers from something called Testicular Feminization Syndrome (TFS) from birth:[1] This is precisely the effect in testicular feminization syndrome -- there are internal, undescended testes and no uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, but externally the labia, vagina, and clitoris all develop. Typically, the labia and clitoris are indistinguishable from those of a normal (46, XX) female, but the vagina is shorter than usual or sometimes absent. Breast development is that of a normal woman, and so are many other sexual characteristics of body habitus, such as pelvic shape. On the other hand, armpit and pubic hair are markedly decreased or even absent. And very importantly: patients with TFS cannot have children. (And Jamie Lee has indeed stated on various occasions that she biologically cannot have kids.) Often, due to their more boyish looks, TFS patient can grow up to be more beautiful than “ordinary” woman, and Jamie is the pinnacle of this formalism. Personally, I do not care at all what her congenital disorder is, because she looks the way she looks, whatever defect is hiding deep inside. (Especially in the 1985 movie Perfect she/he really looked absolutely perfect to me. She never called though.) On the other hand, some people are really disturbed by the very fact that biologically Jamie Lee Curtis is not a woman, but who cares ? She looks like a woman, feels like a woman, and smells like a woman. And that’s about all it takes. SOURCES: the footnoted site. (For the photograph: Jamie Lee Curtis, gorgeous, at the 1980 Cannes festival.)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Who has the most surprising net worth?
Answer: The most improbably candidate would be American singer Dave Matthews. Matthews (who is of South-African descent) and his band are virtually unknown outside of the US — I literally personally do not know anyone in Europe who knows this guy — but in the US, he is an absolute superstar:[1] During the period from 2000 to 2010, his band sold more tickets and earned more money than any other act in North America. Furthermore, the band's 2012 album Away from the World made The Dave Matthews Band (DMB) the only group to have six consecutive studio albums debut at number one on the Billboard charts, and this record was extended even further with the 2018 release of Come Tomorrow. His net worth ? A staggering $300 million dollars.[2] The DMB is a jam band with an almost unmatched live reputation, having released 85 live albums as of today (which sell really good), most of them under DMB’s own Bama Rags label.[3] I happened to see them a couple of months ago, and they blew us away. Matthews also owns ATO Records (which is part of his BMG label). He loves to play and record and does it all the time, but he is also the guy in control — the musical brain who gets the dough in the end. You wouldn’t give it to him — he is nice, idealistic, a bit autistic and weird, introvert, likes to help people and hates people who hate people (hopefully not including himself) — but this man has it all. And he easily beats most Hollywood actors, producers and directors, and singer/songwriters at the heart of their very own game — Olympic Dollar Counting (Paris, 2024). SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the photograph: Rick Wood/Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Who saved your life without even knowing it?
Answer: My mother-in-law is a retired radiologist, and only recently she told us a story about her biggest “mistake” as a doctor. One of her patients suffered from severe pain in one of his collarbones, and he needed a series of medical images be taken to see what was going on. When she was making the images, my mother-in-law slipped and accidentally made images of one of the patient’s lungs. Before deleting the images — which many radiologists unfortunately do with flawed images before even looking at them — she peeped at one of the images without thinking, and noticed a large dark mass in the lung. A lung tumor the size of a plum — this patient had been suffering from lung cancer without knowing it ! The tumor was operable, and the cancer hadn’t spread yet — and in the end, after surgery and chemo, the patient was declared to be in complete remission. If my mother-in-law hadn’t slipped, if she hadn’t taken the accidental images of his lung and taken a quick peek, the cancer would almost surely have been detected in a more advanced stage which would have destroyed his future. But she did. SOURCES: Volume Rendering of a contrast enhanced abdominal CT scan. Rendering done with a Carestream workstation. (Through Google images.)

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: My son got sentenced to 15 years in prison. He is 20 years old. I don’t want him to feel depressed and give up. Is there anything I can do for him while he is in prison?
Answer: My grandfather was imprisoned in a concentration camp in the second World War, and he spent the better part of three years in that camp. He survived it in the end, but lost one lung and a most of his smiles by the time he got out. In the camp, he obviously was never visited by his loved ones, but in some way he virtually was — he received letters from his wife (the paternal grandmother whom I would never meet), and through these letters news about his two young boys (one of whom was my father). A second thing which saved his life — apart from the fact that my grandfather was an exceptionally determined man who proved to be almost impossible to break (his mind was impenetrable) — was the power of reading. In the camp, he learnt German very quickly, and he started to read German books whenever he could. And in some sense, he found a way to escape the horror of the camp through the power of words. And he made it. Your boy on the other hand is still very young — barely adult — and 15 years is a very long time (although we can hope his sentence be eventually reduced if that would be possible), but you can make a huge difference. You are one of very few people who can help him survive being caged for whatever he has done. Visit him as much as you can, write him letters, and keep contact through social media whenever this is possible. Send photographs of the things he misses (even if they are trivial), and talk to him every which way. And send him books — even when he hates to read. He’ll fight you in the beginning, but especially in confinement, reading is more useful than most anything else, and it is perhaps the only way to escape being on the inside. In between the letters, he will be as free as a bird. So encourage him to read your letters and to write letters himself, and convince him to start reading books, even when he thinks he hates them. Once he is in, he will discover the true magic of the way letters dance in books to form words, sentences and stories to take him far away from his prison cell, and make him forget about the cage he is in. Because that’s what letters can do, if combined well enough to form the magical bridge between the paper and sheer fantasy, as if a dancing dervish is whirling his mysterious ways into your head to let the bad stuff out — If even for a very short while. SOURCES: GIF found through Tenor.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What is the most heartbreaking message/text you ever received?
Answer: It was the first weekend of September in 2022. The weather was splendid, and I was working on my laptop in the shadow of our old cedar tree. A text message came in, and a new shadow was cast. It was my friend Anne, who once had been a colleague for more than ten years, but whom I already knew well before she became a colleague. “Hi Thomas. I’m not sure you already heard, but your ex-wife died a couple of days ago. Thought you wanted to know.” Heartbreaking was not the word — my heart had been broken a long time ago when she filed for divorce after a dark period in which she had hidden her cheating through six months of lying — but that scar was gone. And the divide between us was way too deep afterwards for new scars. But it was shocking nonetheless. (My girlfriend became very silent when I told her the news. She had never known my ex-wife personally, but she did know that there were also two young kids with a trauma for life.) Only slightly more than two months ago I had seen my ex-wife for the last time — the very last time, as it now had become clear (and which was weird in itself). I was ordering coffee (and soda) in a coffee shop, and I noticed a woman standing next in line. She looked like a ghost, because every trace of life in this woman was gone. She was staring into nothingness — with glassy, dull and empty eyes — jaundiced, strange and unrecognizable. As if something was coming which was impossible to avert. And I know it was her. And only then I realized how bad her condition was, that the cancer had spread to her liver, and that she was succumbing to her destiny. (As an ex-partner, you only hear so much.) She had noticed me as well, but we did not speak. Ever again. SOURCES: painting by Beksiński.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: Why do some people act less intelligent than they really are?
Answer: I once had a girlfriend who systematically acted less intelligent than she really was, especially when her friends and family were near. Her main reason to do so was that she wanted to fit in, and to some extent I understood her. Because actually, she needed to fit in. Her parents — my neighbors, alas — were, and are, “common sense people.” They never read a book, are not interested in culture whatsoever, hate Nature (I will come back to this interesting feature in a minute), hate intellectuals, and Science in general. “Common sense” is their Science, your honor. And thinking is a city in China. When her father tries to talk to me about our trees — this is the big problem, we have trees in our garden ! — it feels like talking to a wall. An aggressive wall, that is. (He becomes frantic if he finds leaves and twigs in his cement garden, and so does his wife.) He does not listen to what you say, even if he would be able to understand what you are saying. (He’s not.) He lives in this entirely fabricated delusional world, by his own “common sense” rules. And that is the world in which Ebba grew up — constantly fighting against her father’s one-dimensional reasoning, against his bullying and stupidity. Her mom is much friendlier, but intellectually much alike her husband.
